subject: Surgery
title: Wound Healing and Management
objectives: Describe the components and phases of wound healing and their timing.
Distinguish healing by primary, secondary and tertiary intention.
List the general and local factors that impair wound healing.
Differentiate hypertrophic scar, keloid and contracture and outline their treatment.
Classify closed and open wounds by mechanism and predict their risks.
Apply the principles of first aid and theatre management of an open wound.
Recognise the three common chronic wounds and select appropriate sutures and dressings.

sections.title: Components & stages of healing
sections.digest: Injury triggers an ordered cascade of cellular and biochemical events ending in a healed wound. Healing has three **components**: **wound contraction** (myofibroblasts containing smooth-muscle actin, starting at once and continuing 2–3 weeks), **granulation tissue** formation (later replaced by fibrous tissue), and **epithelialisation** (a clean sutured wound epithelialises in about 48 hours). Their proportions differ with wound type: apposed edges heal mostly by epithelialisation with little contraction, whereas a gaping wound relies heavily on contraction and granulation. The process runs through three overlapping **phases**. The **haemostasis and inflammatory phase** (about 5 days) begins with platelet aggregation on subendothelial collagen and activation of the coagulation cascade; platelets release cytokines and growth factors that recruit leucocytes, macrophages and lymphocytes, and **macrophages** drive phagocytosis, debridement and further growth-factor release. In the **proliferative phase** fibroblasts secrete collagen, endothelial cells form capillary buds (together making granulation tissue), and epithelial cells migrate from the edges. In the **maturation/remodelling phase** collagen III is progressively replaced by collagen I, fibres thicken and align along stress lines, and tensile strength rises over roughly a year but never reaches normal.
highYield: Three components: contraction, granulation, epithelialisation.
Clean sutured wound epithelialises in ~48 hours.
Macrophage is the key orchestrating cell of healing.
Collagen III laid first, then replaced by collagen I during remodelling.
~20% of final strength at 3 weeks; ~80% of original at 3 months; never 100%.

tables.title: The three phases of wound healing
rows: Collagen, capillary buds → granulation tissue, epithelial migration
Collagen III → collagen I, fibres align, tensile strength rises

pitfalls: Epithelialisation ≠ return of strength: the wound looks closed at 48 h but is mechanically weak for weeks.
A wound never regains full original tensile strength — do not state 100%.

figures.alt: Three-panel diagram of the stages of wound healing.
figures.described: Three cross-sections of skin across a wound. Panel 1: a fresh gap filled with clot and inflammatory cells invading. Panel 2: new capillaries plus fibroblasts forming red granulation tissue with epithelium starting to creep in from the edges. Panel 3: a healed wound with mature collagen fibres reoriented across the line of the wound.

sections.title: Types of healing (intention)
sections.digest: Wounds heal by one of three **intentions**. **Primary intention**: a clean wound with edges immediately apposed by sutures or clips; minimal granulation and **minimal fibrosis** give a fine neat scar. **Secondary intention**: edges are not apposed or the wound gapes (often after infection); the defect fills with granulation tissue, producing more fibrous tissue and an ugly scar that is devoid of sweat glands, sebaceous glands and hair. **Tertiary intention** (delayed primary closure): a contaminated wound is deliberately left open for about 5 days and, if no infection supervenes, closed with delayed primary sutures.
highYield: Primary = apposed edges, minimal fibrosis, fine scar.
Secondary = gaping/infected, fills with granulation, ugly scar without adnexa.
Tertiary = delayed primary closure of a contaminated wound after ~5 days.

tables.title: Healing by intention
rows: Clean wound, edges apposed at once
Contaminated wound left open ~5 days then closed

pitfalls: Tertiary intention is not the same as secondary: the wound is still surgically closed, just after a delay.

sections.title: Factors affecting healing
sections.digest: Factors are **general** or **local**. General: advanced **age** (slower protein turnover); poor **nutrition** — protein deficiency reduces collagen and ground substance, **vitamin C** deficiency blocks collagen maturation, **vitamin A** deficiency impairs epithelialisation, and deficiencies of zinc, copper, calcium and manganese all delay healing; debilitating disease (uraemia, jaundice, cirrhosis, **diabetes**, malignancy); and drugs — **steroids**, chemotherapy and immunosuppressants. Local: **vascularity** (rich supply of face/scalp heals fast, poor supply below the knee heals slowly), **irradiation** (endarteritis obliterans → ischaemia), **immobilisation** (movement/shear damages granulation tissue, so immobilisation helps), **tension** (sutures under tension, haematoma and infection raise wound tension → ischaemia), **infection** (bacteria compete for oxygen and secrete collagen-destroying enzymes), **foreign bodies and necrotic tissue**, **adhesion to bone** (prevents contraction, e.g. over the shin), and **impaired venous drainage** (post-phlebitic limb).
highYield: Vitamin C → collagen maturation; vitamin A → epithelialisation.
Steroids, diabetes, infection, ischaemia and tension are the classic delayers.
Immobilisation HELPS healing (protects granulation tissue).
Recall these factors when reasoning about burst abdomen and incisional/recurrent hernia.

tables.title: Factors delaying wound healing
rows: Old age; protein/vitamin C/vitamin A/trace-element deficiency
Adhesion to bone; impaired venous drainage

pitfalls: Vitamin C and vitamin A act at different steps — do not swap them.
Movement is bad but immobilisation is good; students often reverse this.

sections.title: Complications & scars
sections.digest: Complications include **wound failure (dehiscence)**: adverse general or local factors cause failure of an abdominal wound → **burst abdomen** or **incisional hernia**. Scar problems: **stretching** of the scar; **hypertrophic scar** — raised but staying *within* the wound margins, may regress within months, common over shoulder and presternum; and **keloid** — overactive healing with excess scar that extends *beyond* the original wound, follows burns/trauma/surgery/ear-piercing/vaccination, commoner in dark skin with familial predisposition, and favours ear lobules, shoulder and presternal skin. **Contracture** is pathological shortening of scar tissue causing deformity when a scar crosses a joint; correct joint positioning during healing minimises it. Treatment of hypertrophic scars and keloids: silicone-gel-sheet **pressure**, **intralesional triamcinolone**, and **surgical excision** (recurrence after simple excision may reach 80%, so use intramarginal excision plus intra-operative steroid).
highYield: Hypertrophic scar stays WITHIN the wound; keloid extends BEYOND it.
Keloid: dark skin, familial, ear lobules/shoulder/presternum.
Contracture crosses joints → deformity; position the joint correctly while healing.
Keloid excision alone recurs up to ~80% → combine excision with steroid.
pitfalls: “Raised scar” is not automatically a keloid — the discriminator is whether it stays within (hypertrophic) or grows beyond (keloid) the wound.

sections.title: Closed wounds
sections.digest: A closed wound leaves skin intact. A **contusion** (bruise) follows a blunt blow that extravasates blood through injured capillaries; the area is painful and swollen, bluish then brown/green as blood breaks down. Elevation and a topical anti-inflammatory help. A **haematoma** forms when bleeding is excessive: initially cystic, it clots within hours and later liquefies. A small haematoma may be aspirated with a wide-bore needle; otherwise it is evacuated by incision under aseptic technique.
highYield: Contusion colour evolves bluish → brown/green.
Small haematoma → aspirate; large → formal incision and evacuation.

sections.title: Open wounds
sections.digest: Open wounds breach the skin. **Abrasion**: superficial layers scraped off by friction; very painful (exposed nerve endings); clean with a bland antiseptic and a non-adherent dressing. **Incised**: clean-cut by a sharp blade; longer than deep, minimal tissue destruction but brisk haemorrhage and risk to tendons/nerves. **Lacerated**: blunt severe violence (road traffic accidents, falls); irregular, devitalised, contaminated, high infection risk; inflammatory oedema raises wound tension and causes secondary ischaemia, and a **degloving injury** may strip skin and fat off the deep fascia — devascularisation appears over the next few days. **Penetrating**: a pointed object; deeper than long, small external opening with poor drainage encouraging infection; deceptive — always suspect deep-structure injury. **Missile**: a bullet transmits high kinetic energy (KE = ½MV², so velocity dominates — rifles far worse than pistols); damage from the direct track, shock waves, temporary cavitation, and secondary bony fragments. Structures far from the tract may be injured. **Bites** (animal/human) are lacerated, contaminated and highly infective.
highYield: Incised = longer than deep; penetrating = deeper than long.
KE = ½MV² → velocity matters most; high-velocity (rifle) >> low-velocity (pistol).
Penetrating wound: always suspect deep injury; a stab of the abdominal wall may hide a visceral injury.
Lacerated wounds are commonly accompanied by degloving; reassess viability over days.

tables.title: Open wound types
rows: Longer than deep, brisk bleed, tendon/nerve risk
Deeper than long, poor drainage, hidden deep injury
Track + shock wave + cavitation + secondary fragments

pitfalls: In missile injury, damage can occur far from the visible tract — do not limit exploration to the entry track.

sections.title: Management of open wounds
sections.digest: **First aid**: treat as a multiple-injury patient; take a timing/mechanism history to predict injured structures; give **tetanus prophylaxis** and prophylactic antibiotics (add anaerobic cover for deep/lacerated wounds); control bleeding by direct compression with a sterile dressing and firm bandage (a tourniquet only as a temporary measure before theatre); X-ray and splint suspected fractures; and feel distal pulses (urgent duplex if absent). **In theatre**: thorough saline **irrigation** and meticulous removal of foreign bodies, then antiseptic (e.g. povidone-iodine). Repair a major artery/vein; ligate small vessels. Repair nerves/tendons in clean incised wounds but **defer** in contaminated wounds. Repair clean muscle with mattress sutures; excise ischaemic/necrotic muscle (dark/grey, does not contract when pinched or bleed when cut). In contaminated wounds or extensive tissue loss leave the **deep fascia open**. Skin: clean and early (<6 h) → primary closure; contaminated/late → delayed primary closure; lacerations → debride to healthy tissue; degloving of doubtful viability → second look at 3–4 days. Stabilise associated fractures by **external** fixation when infection is possible (internal fixation would seed bone). All missile injuries require exploration.
highYield: Contaminated wound rule: do NOT repair nerve/tendon, do NOT close deep fascia, do NOT close skin.
Clean & early (<6 h) → primary closure; late/contaminated → delayed primary closure.
Necrotic muscle: dark/grey, no contraction on pinch, no bleeding on cut → excise.
Possible infection + fracture → external fixation, not internal.

tables.title: Skin closure decision
rows: Leave open, second look at 3–4 days

pitfalls: A stab wound of the abdominal wall can be sutured while a visceral injury is missed — do not close a penetrating wound without excluding deep injury.
Internal fixation in a potentially infected field spreads infection to bone.

sections.title: Chronic wounds
sections.digest: A **chronic wound** fails the normal healing sequence within a reasonable time (about three months), arrested at the inflammatory/proliferative phase by factors such as ischaemia, venous congestion, diabetes, steroids or necrotic tissue; most share local hypoxia. Manage the general factors hand-in-hand with local wound care. Three categories recur. **Chronic leg ulcers** (ulcer = a break in the continuity of epithelium/mucosa): the commonest are **venous** ulcers; others are ischaemic, neuropathic and neoplastic (squamous or, rarely, basal cell carcinoma). **Diabetic foot ulcers**. **Pressure sores** (bed/decubitus ulcers) develop in bedridden patients from sustained skin pressure; risk factors include old age, poor nutrition, anaemia, denervation, paraplegia, ICU stay, immobilisation and soiling by urine/stool; common sites are ischial tuberosity, greater trochanter, sacrum, heel and malleoli; they progress through erythema → partial-thickness loss → full-thickness loss short of the fascia → deeper destruction into muscle, bone and joints. Prevention/treatment: correct general factors, regular turning, dry skin, air mattresses, debridement, vacuum-assisted closure and flap cover.
highYield: Chronic wound = fails to heal within ~3 months; shares local hypoxia.
Venous ulcer is the commonest chronic leg ulcer.
Pressure sore sites: ischial tuberosity, greater trochanter, sacrum, heel, malleoli.
A long-standing ulcer can undergo malignant (usually squamous cell) change.
pitfalls: Non-healing chronic ulcer with heaped edges → biopsy for malignant change.

sections.title: Suture materials
sections.digest: Sutures appose wound edges until healing occurs and are classified by **origin** (natural/synthetic), **absorption** (absorbable/non-absorbable — the most important axis) and **mode of synthesis** (**monofilament** vs **multifilament/braided**). Natural materials provoke more tissue reaction and can maintain infection; multifilament sutures react more and, in infection, can harbour ~10× more organisms than an equivalent monofilament because capillary spaces between filaments let organisms settle. **Absorbable**: chromic catgut (natural, absorbed ~3 weeks, largely obsolete); **polyglycolic acid (Dexon)** and **polyglactin (Vicryl)** (braided synthetics for GI/soft tissue, absorbed over 2–4 months); **polydioxanone (PDS)** (monofilament, slowest to absorb). **Non-absorbable**: **silk** (braided protein, marked reaction, actually very slowly absorbable); **polyamide/nylon** (mono or multi, good strength, insecure knot); **polypropylene (Prolene)** (monofilament, inert, ideal for abdominal wall and hernia repair, needs no removal if infected but knots poorly); **stainless steel** (very strong and inert, difficult handling, used to close sternotomy). Other skin closure: clips, staplers, adhesive tapes (no tissue reaction) and skin glue.
highYield: Absorbable vs non-absorbable is the most important classification.
Monofilament resists infection better than braided (no capillary spaces).
PDS is the slowest-absorbing absorbable; Prolene is ideal for abdominal wall/hernia.
Silk is technically slowly absorbable despite being classed non-absorbable.
pitfalls: In a contaminated field prefer monofilament — braided suture sustains infection.
Vicryl/Dexon (synthetic braided) are ABSORBABLE; silk (natural braided) is non-absorbable — do not group by braiding.

figures.alt: Cross-section of monofilament vs braided suture.
figures.described: Two magnified cross-sections: on the left a single smooth circular strand (monofilament); on the right many small strands bundled together with capillary gaps between them (braided/multifilament), the gaps where organisms can lodge.

sections.title: Wound dressings
sections.digest: Dressings provide the ideal environment for healing and limit bacterial overgrowth. **Occlusive** dressings (gauze + adhesive plaster) protect the wound and prevent evaporation, maintaining hydration; local hypoxia favours capillary proliferation and autolysis of slough, but they are unsuitable for infected or highly exudative wounds. **Semi-occlusive** dressings (e.g. hydrocolloid sheets) are permeable to water vapour and gases but not bacteria and keep a moist bed. **Alginates** (from seaweed) form a fibrous gel on contact with exudate. **Osmotic agents** (Debrisan, urea crystals, honey) absorb exudate. Two measures enhance the whole process: **vacuum-assisted closure (VAC)**, whose negative pressure promotes granulation and contraction (good for pressure sores and diabetic ulcers), and increased local hydration for moist healing.
highYield: Occlusive dressings are unsuitable for infected/highly exudative wounds.
Alginates are seaweed-derived and gel with exudate.
VAC uses negative pressure to boost granulation and contraction; good for pressure sores/diabetic ulcers.

tables.title: Wound dressings
rows: Protects, retains moisture; not for infected/exudative wounds
Vapour/gas permeable, bacteria impermeable, moist bed

pitfalls: Do not put an occlusive dressing on an infected or heavily exudative wound.

cards.front: Name the three components of wound healing.
cards.back: Wound contraction, granulation tissue formation and epithelialisation.

cards.front: Which cell drives wound contraction and what protein does it contain?
cards.back: The myofibroblast, which contains the smooth-muscle protein actin.

cards.cloze: Wound contraction starts immediately and continues for about {{c1::2–3 weeks}}.

cards.front: How long does a clean sutured wound take to epithelialise?
cards.back: About 48 hours.

cards.cloze: Granulation tissue is later replaced by {{c1::fibrous tissue}}.

cards.front: List the three phases of wound healing in order.
cards.back: Haemostasis & inflammation, proliferation, then maturation & remodelling.

cards.front: How long does the haemostasis and inflammatory phase normally last?
cards.back: About 5 days.

cards.front: What starts the haemostasis phase at the injured vessel?
cards.back: Platelet aggregation on subendothelial collagen and activation of the coagulation cascade.

cards.front: Which cell is central to phagocytosis and debridement and releases growth factors to recruit fibroblasts?
cards.back: The macrophage.

cards.front: In the proliferative phase, what do fibroblasts and endothelial cells together form?
cards.back: Granulation tissue (collagen from fibroblasts plus new capillary buds).

cards.cloze: Young epithelium is thinner than normal and has no {{c1::sebaceous glands, sweat glands or hair follicles}}.

cards.front: Which collagen type is deposited first, and what replaces it during remodelling?
cards.back: Collagen III first; it is progressively replaced by collagen I.

cards.cloze: Remodelling continues for about {{c1::one year}}, and the wound never regains full original tensile strength.

cards.front: What proportion of final strength does a wound have at 3 weeks?
cards.back: About 20%.

cards.front: What proportion of original strength does a wound have at 3 months?
cards.back: About 80% — and it never regains 100%.

cards.front: Single word: the cell orchestrating wound healing.
cards.back: macrophage

cards.front: Define healing by primary intention.
cards.back: A clean wound with edges apposed at once (sutures/clips), healing with minimal fibrosis and a fine scar.

cards.front: Define healing by secondary intention.
cards.back: Unapposed or gaping wound (often infected) that fills with granulation tissue → more fibrosis and an ugly scar.

cards.front: Define healing by tertiary intention.
cards.back: Delayed primary closure: a contaminated wound left open ~5 days then sutured if no infection appears.

cards.cloze: A secondary-intention scar is devoid of {{c1::sweat glands, sebaceous glands and hair}}.

cards.front: Delayed primary closure of a contaminated wound after ~5 days
cards.back: Healing by tertiary intention

cards.front: A clean wound closed immediately heals by which intention? (one word)
cards.back: primary

cards.front: How does vitamin C deficiency impair healing?
cards.back: It prevents maturation of protocollagen (collagen maturation).

cards.front: How does vitamin A deficiency impair healing?
cards.back: It causes deficient epithelialisation.

cards.cloze: Wound healing is slow in the elderly because of a reduced rate of {{c1::protein turnover}}.

cards.front: Name three drug classes that inhibit wound healing.
cards.back: Steroids, cancer chemotherapy and immunosuppressants.

cards.front: Which trace elements, if deficient, delay healing?
cards.back: Zinc, copper, calcium and manganese.

cards.front: Why does immobilisation help wound healing?
cards.back: Movement and shear damage the blood supply of granulation tissue; immobilisation protects it.

cards.front: How does irradiation impair healing?
cards.back: Endarteritis obliterans causes ischaemia, impairing contraction and granulation.

cards.front: Give two ways infection delays healing.
cards.back: Bacteria compete with fibroblasts for oxygen/nutrition and secrete enzymes that destroy collagen.

cards.cloze: A good blood supply (face and scalp) heals fast, whereas a poor supply below the {{c1::knee}} heals slowly.

cards.front: Why do wounds over the shin of the tibia contract poorly?
cards.back: Adhesion of the wound to the underlying bone prevents contraction.

cards.front: Which three conditions typically apply when studying burst abdomen and hernia recurrence?
cards.back: The factors that impair wound healing — review them together.

cards.front: Failure of an abdominal wound leads to which two problems?
cards.back: Burst abdomen or incisional hernia.

cards.front: Key difference between a hypertrophic scar and a keloid?
cards.back: Hypertrophic stays within the wound margins; keloid extends beyond them.

cards.cloze: Keloids are commoner in {{c1::dark}} skin and have a familial predisposition.

cards.front: Name three sites prone to keloid formation.
cards.back: Ear lobules, shoulder and presternal area.

cards.front: What is a contracture and where does it cause problems?
cards.back: Pathological shortening of scar tissue causing deformity when a scar overlies a joint.

cards.front: Three treatments for hypertrophic scars and keloids?
cards.back: Silicone-gel-sheet pressure, intralesional triamcinolone and surgical excision (with steroid).

cards.cloze: Recurrence after simple excision of a keloid may reach {{c1::80%}}, so combine intramarginal excision with steroid.

cards.front: Raised scar that extends beyond the original wound margins
cards.back: Keloid

cards.front: How does the colour of a contusion evolve?
cards.back: Bluish (extravasated blood) then brownish or green as it breaks down.

cards.front: How is a small haematoma managed versus a large one?
cards.back: Small → aspirate with a wide-bore needle; large → evacuate by incision under aseptic technique.

cards.cloze: A haematoma is at first cystic, clots within {{c1::hours}}, then later liquefies.

cards.front: Why is an abrasion so painful?
cards.back: The superficial skin is scraped off, exposing sensitive nerve endings.

cards.front: Describe an incised wound.
cards.back: Clean-cut by a sharp blade, longer than deep, little tissue destruction, brisk bleeding, tendon/nerve risk.

cards.cloze: A penetrating wound is {{c1::deeper than long}}, so always suspect injury to deep structures.

cards.front: What is a degloving injury?
cards.back: Shearing that strips an area of skin and subcutaneous fat off the underlying deep fascia.

cards.front: Give the kinetic energy formula for a missile and its clinical implication.
cards.back: KE = ½MV²; velocity dominates, so high-velocity rifle wounds are far worse than low-velocity pistol wounds.

cards.front: List the mechanisms of tissue damage in a missile wound.
cards.back: Direct track damage, shock waves, temporary cavitation, and secondary bony fragments.

cards.cloze: In missile injury, structures {{c1::far from the tract}} may be injured.

cards.front: Why are bites high-risk wounds?
cards.back: They are lacerated and contaminated with a high incidence of infection.

cards.front: An incised wound is longer than ____ (one word).
cards.back: deep

cards.front: Two prophylaxis steps in first aid of an open wound?
cards.back: Tetanus prophylaxis and prophylactic antibiotics (anaerobic cover if deep/lacerated).

cards.front: Best first-line method to stop wound bleeding?
cards.back: Direct local compression with a sterile dressing and firm bandage; tourniquet only as a temporary measure before theatre.

cards.front: What must you do if distal pulses are not palpable?
cards.back: Reassess after treating shock; urgent duplex is mandatory if still absent.

cards.front: How is necrotic muscle recognised intra-operatively?
cards.back: Dark red or grey, does not contract when pinched, and does not bleed when incised → excise it.

cards.cloze: In contaminated wounds, do not repair nerve or tendon, do not close the {{c1::deep fascia}}, and do not close the skin.

cards.front: Clean-and-early (<6 h) skin wound — how is it closed?
cards.back: Primary closure.

cards.front: Contaminated or late skin wound — how is it closed?
cards.back: Delayed primary closure.

cards.front: Degloving injury of doubtful skin viability — what is the plan?
cards.back: Leave the decision to a second look at 3–4 days.

cards.front: Why use external rather than internal fixation when infection is possible?
cards.back: Internal fixation would spread infection to bone.

cards.front: Which wounds always require exploration?
cards.back: All missile injuries.

cards.front: Do not repair nerve/tendon, do not close deep fascia or skin
cards.back: Rules for a contaminated wound

cards.front: How is a chronic wound defined?
cards.back: One that fails the normal healing sequence within a reasonable time — usually about three months.

cards.front: What do most chronic wounds share locally?
cards.back: Local hypoxia (from ischaemia, trauma, vasculitis).

cards.front: What is the commonest type of chronic leg ulcer?
cards.back: Venous ulcer.

cards.front: Define an ulcer.
cards.back: A break in the continuity of epithelium or mucous membrane.

cards.front: Which malignancies can arise in a chronic leg ulcer?
cards.back: Squamous cell carcinoma (Marjolin's) or, rarely, basal cell carcinoma.

cards.cloze: Common pressure-sore sites are the {{c1::ischial tuberosity}}, greater trochanter, sacrum, heel and malleoli.

cards.front: List the four stages of a pressure sore.
cards.back: Erythema → partial-thickness loss → full-thickness loss short of fascia → destruction into muscle/bone/joint.

cards.front: Name four risk factors for pressure sores.
cards.back: Old age, poor nutrition, anaemia, immobilisation (also denervation, paraplegia, ICU stay, soiling).

cards.front: Two dressing/device measures that help pressure sores heal?
cards.back: Vacuum-assisted closure and air mattresses (plus turning, debridement, flaps).

cards.front: What is the single most important way to classify a suture?
cards.back: By absorption — absorbable versus non-absorbable.

cards.front: Why does a braided suture sustain infection more than a monofilament?
cards.back: Capillary spaces between filaments let organisms settle — up to ~10× more than an equivalent monofilament.

cards.front: Which absorbable suture is the slowest to absorb?
cards.back: Polydioxanone (PDS), a monofilament.

cards.front: Name a braided absorbable suture used for GI anastomoses.
cards.back: Polyglactin (Vicryl) — or polyglycolic acid (Dexon).

cards.cloze: {{c1::Polypropylene (Prolene)}} is a monofilament, very inert, and ideal for abdominal wall and hernia repair.

cards.front: Why is silk unusual among non-absorbable sutures?
cards.back: It is a braided protein that provokes marked reaction and is in fact very slowly absorbable.

cards.front: Which suture closes a sternotomy in open-heart surgery?
cards.back: Stainless steel.

cards.front: A drawback of polyamide (nylon)?
cards.back: The knot is not very secure.

cards.front: Why do adhesive skin tapes cause no inflammatory reaction?
cards.back: No suture material transverses the skin.

cards.front: Slowest-absorbing absorbable suture (abbreviation).
cards.back: PDS

cards.front: Why are occlusive dressings unsuitable for some wounds?
cards.back: They are unsuitable for infected and highly exudative wounds.

cards.front: How does an occlusive dressing aid healing?
cards.back: Prevents evaporation to keep hydration; local hypoxia favours capillary proliferation and autolysis of slough.

cards.front: What are alginate dressings derived from and how do they act?
cards.back: From seaweed; on contact with exudate they form a fibrous gel giving a moist environment.

cards.front: Give two osmotic dressing agents.
cards.back: Debrisan, urea crystals or honey.

cards.front: How does VAC promote healing and where is it especially useful?
cards.back: Negative pressure enhances granulation and stimulates contraction; good for pressure sores and diabetic ulcers.

cards.cloze: Semi-occlusive hydrocolloid dressings are permeable to water vapour and gases but impermeable to {{c1::bacteria}}.

cards.front: From which cells are the cytokines and growth factors of the early phase first released?
cards.back: Platelets.

cards.front: In which intention does wound contraction and granulation contribute most?
cards.back: Secondary intention, when wound edges are wide apart.

cards.cloze: Debilitating diseases that delay healing include uraemia, jaundice, cirrhosis, {{c1::diabetes}} and malignancy.

cards.front: What simple measures help a contusion?
cards.back: Elevation to minimise oedema and a local anti-inflammatory ointment.

cards.front: How is an abrasion dressed?
cards.back: Cleaned with a bland antiseptic and covered with a non-adherent dressing.

cards.front: At which phases are most chronic wounds arrested?
cards.back: The inflammatory and proliferative phases, with minimal contraction and collagen formation.

cards.front: Besides VAC, what second measure enhances the whole healing process?
cards.back: Increased local hydration providing a moist environment (moist healing).

mcqs.stem: A clean surgical incision is closed with sutures. Approximately how long does it take to epithelialise?

options.why: Faster than the usual figure quoted for a clean sutured wound.
Correct — a clean sutured wound epithelialises in about 48 hours.
This is far too long for simple epithelialisation of apposed edges.
At 3 weeks the wound has only ~20% of its final strength; epithelialisation is long complete.
Corresponds to ~80% of strength, not initial epithelialisation.

explanation: Apposed clean edges heal chiefly by epithelialisation.
This is complete in roughly 48 hours.
Strength, however, lags far behind cover.
keyFacts: Clean sutured wound epithelialises in ~48 h.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Epithelial cover is fast; tensile strength is slow.

mcqs.stem: Which cell is chiefly responsible for wound contraction?

options.why: A first-responder inflammatory cell, not the contractile cell.
Orchestrates healing and debridement but does not itself contract the wound.
Correct — it contains smooth-muscle actin and contracts the wound.
Forms capillary buds for granulation tissue, not contraction.
Modulates the immune response; not contractile.

explanation: Wound contraction reduces wound size from the outset.
It is driven by myofibroblasts containing smooth-muscle actin.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Contraction is a myofibroblast function.

mcqs.stem: During remodelling, the change in collagen is best described as:

options.text: Collagen I replaced by collagen III
options.why: This is the reverse of what happens.

options.text: Collagen III replaced by collagen I
options.why: Correct — immature III is progressively replaced by mature I.

options.text: Collagen II replaced by collagen I
options.why: Collagen II is cartilage collagen, not relevant here.
The subtype ratio changes markedly during remodelling.
Elastin does not replace collagen in a scar.

explanation: Collagen III is laid down first.
Over weeks it is replaced by collagen I, which carries tensile strength.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Remodelling swaps collagen III for collagen I.

mcqs.stem: Three months after a laceration, the wound's tensile strength is approximately:

options.why: This corresponds to about 3 weeks, not 3 months.
An intermediate value not quoted for this milestone.
Correct — about 80% at 3 months, and never 100%.
A wound never regains its full original strength.
Scar is weaker, not stronger, than intact tissue.

explanation: At 3 weeks a wound has ~20% of final strength.
By 3 months it reaches ~80% of original — but never fully recovers.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Strength recovery plateaus below normal.

mcqs.stem: A contaminated wound is deliberately left open for five days and then sutured once infection is excluded. This is healing by:

options.why: Primary intention closes clean wounds immediately.
Secondary intention leaves the wound to granulate, not to be sutured later.
Correct — delayed primary closure of a contaminated wound.
Not a recognised category.
Regeneration restores original tissue without scar; not applicable here.

explanation: Delayed primary closure = tertiary intention.
The wound is watched ~5 days, then closed if clean.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Contaminated wounds are best closed after a delay.

mcqs.stem: A raised scar over the earlobe after piercing extends well beyond the original wound margins. The most likely diagnosis is:

options.why: A hypertrophic scar stays within the wound margins.
Correct — growth beyond the wound margins, classic at the earlobe.
A contracture shortens tissue across a joint, not this appearance.
That is malignant change in a chronic wound, not a raised scar.
A normal scar does not overgrow the wound boundary.

explanation: The discriminator is the wound margin.
Extension beyond it defines a keloid; the earlobe is a classic site.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Site plus overgrowth points to keloid.

mcqs.stem: Which treatment strategy minimises recurrence after excision of a keloid?

options.why: Recurrence may reach ~80% with excision alone.
Correct — combining excision with steroid reduces recurrence.

options.text: Wide excision with primary closure under tension
options.why: Tension worsens scarring and recurrence.
Not the standard first strategy described here.
Keloids do not reliably regress like hypertrophic scars.

explanation: Excision alone recurs frequently.
Intramarginal excision plus steroid is recommended.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Keloid excision needs adjuvant steroid.

mcqs.stem: A patient on long-term corticosteroids heals poorly. Which additional deficiency specifically impairs collagen maturation?

options.why: Vitamin A deficiency impairs epithelialisation, not collagen maturation.
Correct — vitamin C is needed for maturation of protocollagen.
Vitamin K affects clotting factors, not collagen maturation.
Vitamin D governs calcium/bone, not collagen cross-linking here.
B12 affects haematopoiesis/neurology, not collagen maturation.

explanation: Vitamin C is required for collagen (protocollagen) maturation.
Vitamin A, by contrast, supports epithelialisation.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Match the vitamin to its healing step.

mcqs.stem: Which local factor actually FAVOURS wound healing?

options.why: Infection delays healing.
Tension causes ischaemia and impairs healing.
Correct — it protects granulation tissue from shear.
Foreign material impairs healing.
Irradiation causes ischaemia via endarteritis obliterans.

explanation: Movement and shear damage granulation tissue.
Immobilisation therefore aids healing.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Protecting granulation tissue speeds healing.

mcqs.stem: A stab wound to the anterior abdominal wall looks small and shallow. The safest principle is:

options.why: This risks missing a visceral injury beneath a deceptive wound.

options.text: Assume no deep injury if the opening is small
options.why: A small opening does not exclude deep injury in penetrating wounds.
Correct — penetrating wounds are deceptive; suspect deep injury.
Inappropriate for an abdominal-wall stab.
Delaying assessment risks a missed viscus injury.

explanation: A penetrating wound is deeper than long with a small opening.
An unwary surgeon may close it and miss an injured viscus.
keyFacts: Penetrating wound → always suspect deep injury.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Never close a stab without excluding deep injury.

mcqs.stem: Why are high-velocity rifle wounds far more destructive than low-velocity pistol wounds?

options.text: Because kinetic energy depends mainly on mass
options.why: KE depends on the square of velocity, not mainly mass.

options.text: Because kinetic energy depends on the square of velocity
options.why: Correct — KE = ½MV², so velocity dominates.
High-velocity rounds cause greater cavitation.
Fragmentation adds to, not subtracts from, damage.

options.text: Because low-velocity rounds cause shock waves
options.why: Shock waves are a feature of high-energy transfer.

explanation: KE = ½MV².
Doubling velocity quadruples energy transferred to tissue.
keyFacts: Velocity is squared in the KE formula.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Velocity is the key determinant of missile injury.

mcqs.stem: In a heavily contaminated wound, which action is correct?

options.why: Contaminated wounds should not have primary skin closure.
Tendon repair is deferred in contaminated wounds.
Correct — deep fascia is left open in contamination/extensive loss.
Closing the deep fascia is contraindicated here.
Internal fixation risks seeding bone with infection.

explanation: Contaminated-wound rule: no nerve/tendon repair, deep fascia and skin left open.
Delayed primary closure is used for skin.
keyFacts: Leave deep fascia and skin open in contamination.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Do not close a contaminated wound primarily.

mcqs.stem: Muscle in the base of a traumatic wound is dark grey, does not contract when pinched and does not bleed when cut. The correct action is:

options.why: Only clean, viable muscle is repaired.

options.text: Leave it and close over it
options.why: Necrotic muscle left in situ becomes a nidus for infection.
Correct — non-viable muscle should be completely excised.
This does not restore viability.

options.text: Cover with a skin graft immediately
options.why: Grafting over dead muscle will fail.

explanation: Viability signs: colour, contraction on pinch, bleeding on cut.
Muscle failing all three is necrotic and must be excised.
keyFacts: Excise muscle that is grey, non-contractile and non-bleeding.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Debride non-viable muscle completely.

mcqs.stem: A limb wound with a fracture is contaminated and infection is possible. Which fixation is preferred?

options.why: Internal fixation would spread infection to bone.
Also internal; risks seeding the medullary canal.
Correct — stabilises the fracture without seeding bone.
The fracture still needs stabilisation.
Inappropriate in a contaminated field.

explanation: Infected/contaminated fields contraindicate internal fixation.
External fixation stabilises without internal hardware in bone.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Avoid internal metal in a dirty field.

mcqs.stem: Which is the commonest type of chronic leg ulcer?

options.why: Important but not the commonest.
Correct — venous ulcers are the commonest chronic leg ulcer.
Common in diabetes but not the overall commonest leg ulcer.
Uncommon; arises from malignant change.
Not a recognised chronic-ulcer category here.

explanation: Chronic leg ulcers are heterogeneous.
The venous type is the commonest.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Think venous first for a chronic leg ulcer.

mcqs.stem: A bedridden elderly patient develops full-thickness skin loss over the sacrum that stops just short of the fascia. This is which pressure-sore stage?

options.why: Stage 1 is erythema with intact skin.
Stage 2 is partial-thickness loss.
Correct — full-thickness loss short of the fascia.
Stage 4 destroys muscle, bone or joint.
The description fits stage 3.

explanation: Staging runs erythema → partial → full-thickness short of fascia → deeper.
Full-thickness but sparing fascia is stage 3.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Grade pressure sores by depth.

mcqs.stem: A chronic non-healing ulcer with raised, everted edges is most concerning for:

options.why: Venous ulcers typically have sloping edges.
Correct — heaped/everted edges suggest Marjolin's (SCC).
Infection alone does not usually give everted edges.
Arterial ulcers are punched-out, not everted.
Healing ulcers have healthy sloping margins.

explanation: A long-standing ulcer can undergo squamous carcinomatous change.
Raised, everted edges are the warning sign → biopsy.
keyFacts: Everted edges in a chronic ulcer → biopsy for SCC.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Chronic ulcers can turn malignant.

mcqs.stem: Which suture is ideal for closure of the abdominal wall and hernia repair?

options.why: Absorbable and largely obsolete; unsuitable for durable closure.
Braided, reactive and slowly absorbable; not ideal here.
Correct — inert monofilament, ideal for abdominal wall/hernia.
Braided absorbable; used for soft tissue/GI, not durable wall closure.
Used for sternotomy, not routine abdominal-wall/hernia repair.

explanation: Prolene is a very inert monofilament.
It is the material of choice for abdominal-wall and hernia repair.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Match suture to task: Prolene for the wall.

mcqs.stem: In the presence of infection, why is a monofilament suture preferred over a braided one?

options.why: Absorption is not the reason and depends on the material.

options.text: It has no capillary spaces to harbour organisms
options.why: Correct — braided sutures wick and shelter organisms.
Strength is not the deciding factor here.
Cost is irrelevant to infection risk.
Not the mechanism at play.

explanation: Braided suture has capillary spaces between filaments.
These can harbour ~10× more organisms than an equivalent monofilament.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Choose monofilament in contaminated fields.

mcqs.stem: Which absorbable suture is the slowest to absorb?

options.why: Absorbs within about 3 weeks.
Absorbs over ~2–3 months.
Absorbs over ~4 months.
Correct — monofilament, the slowest-absorbing absorbable.
Absorbs quickly, not slowly.

explanation: Among absorbables, PDS lasts longest.
It is a monofilament, useful for slow-healing abdominal closure.
mcqs.teachingPoint: PDS gives prolonged absorbable support.

mcqs.stem: Which dressing is LEAST suitable for an infected, highly exudative wound?

options.why: Alginates handle exudate well.
Correct — unsuitable for infected/exudative wounds.
Osmotic agents absorb exudate.
Permeable to vapour, keeps a moist bed.
VAC manages exudate under negative pressure.

explanation: Occlusive dressings retain moisture and cause local hypoxia.
They are therefore unsuitable for infected/highly exudative wounds.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Match the dressing to exudate and infection.

mcqs.stem: How does vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) promote healing?

options.why: VAC uses negative, not positive, pressure.

options.text: Negative pressure enhances granulation and contraction
options.why: Correct — this is the mechanism, useful in pressure/diabetic ulcers.
VAC is a physical, not chemical, therapy.

options.text: It replaces the need for debridement
options.why: Debridement is still required.
It reduces exudate/oedema but does not sterilise.

explanation: VAC applies sub-atmospheric pressure to the wound bed.
This boosts granulation and stimulates contraction.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Negative pressure accelerates a granulating wound.

mcqs.stem: A small, fluctuant collection of blood forms under the skin after blunt trauma and has been present for a few hours. The most appropriate initial management of a SMALL one is:

options.why: Reserved for large haematomas.
Correct — a small haematoma can be aspirated.
May help a contusion but a defined small haematoma is aspirated.
Antibiotics do not evacuate a haematoma.

options.text: Ignore — it will always resorb fully
options.why: Not reliable for a defined collection.

explanation: A haematoma clots then liquefies.
A small one may be aspirated; a large one is incised and evacuated.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Size guides haematoma management.

mcqs.stem: The phase of wound healing dominated by macrophage-driven debridement and lasting about five days is the:

options.why: Proliferation follows inflammation and builds granulation tissue.
Correct — clot, coagulation and macrophage debridement, ~5 days.
Maturation remodels collagen over months.
Not a distinct named phase.
Contraction is a component, not the ~5-day inflammatory phase.

explanation: The first phase combines haemostasis and inflammation.
Macrophages debride and release growth factors over about 5 days.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Inflammation sets up the repair that follows.

mcqs.stem: Which wound is characteristically 'longer than deep' with clean edges and minimal tissue destruction?

options.why: Lacerations are irregular and devitalised.
Correct — a sharp blade gives a clean wound longer than deep.
Penetrating wounds are deeper than long.
An abrasion is a superficial friction wound.
A contusion is a closed bruise.

explanation: Incised wounds are made by sharp blades.
They are longer than deep with clean edges and brisk bleeding.
keyFacts: Incised = longer than deep, clean edges.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Mechanism defines wound morphology.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about wound-healing factors is TRUE?

options.why: Steroids inhibit healing.
Correct.
Good vascularity speeds healing.
Infection destroys collagen and delays healing.
Tension causes ischaemia.

explanation: Sort each factor into helps vs harms.
Vitamin A deficiency impairs epithelialisation — the only true option.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Know the direction of each healing factor.

mcqs.stem: Which feature best distinguishes a scar healed by secondary intention?

options.why: That describes primary intention.

options.text: Ugly wide scar lacking sweat/sebaceous glands and hair
options.why: Correct — secondary-intention scar features.
Secondary intention always scars.
That is primary intention.
That is tertiary intention.

explanation: Secondary intention fills a gap with granulation tissue.
The resulting scar is wide and devoid of skin adnexa.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Granulation-filled wounds scar poorly.

mcqs.stem: Failure of an abdominal surgical wound may present as:

options.why: Keloid is a scar problem, not wound failure of the abdomen.
Correct — the two classic consequences.
Contracture affects scars over joints.
A scar issue, not dehiscence.
That is malignant change in a chronic wound.

explanation: Adverse factors can cause abdominal wound failure.
This presents as burst abdomen or later incisional hernia.
keyFacts: Abdominal wound failure → burst abdomen/incisional hernia.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Dehiscence has early and late forms.

mcqs.stem: Which is the best first-line method to control bleeding from an open wound in first aid?

options.why: Only a temporary measure before theatre, not first-line.

options.text: Direct compression with sterile dressing and firm bandage
options.why: Correct — first-line haemostasis.
Risks damaging nerves/vessels.
Helpful adjunct but not the primary method described.
Not the first mechanical step for external bleeding.

explanation: External wound bleeding is first controlled mechanically.
Direct compression with a sterile dressing and bandage is first-line; a tourniquet is only temporary.
keyFacts: Direct compression first; tourniquet only temporarily.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Compress before you consider a tourniquet.

mcqs.stem: A patient is thrown from a motorcycle; an area of thigh skin and fat is sheared off the deep fascia, with skin viability doubtful. This injury is best termed:

options.why: Incised wounds are clean sharp cuts.
Correct — skin/fat stripped off deep fascia.
Abrasions are superficial friction wounds.
A contusion is a closed bruise.
A puncture is a deep narrow track.

explanation: Blunt shear can strip skin/fat off the deep fascia.
Viability is judged at a second look after 3–4 days.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Doubtful degloved skin is reassessed, not discarded.

mcqs.stem: Which suture is a braided natural material that provokes marked tissue reaction yet is technically very slowly absorbable?

options.why: Prolene is an inert synthetic monofilament.
Correct — braided protein, reactive, slowly absorbable.
PDS is a synthetic absorbable monofilament.
Nylon is a synthetic polyamide.
Steel is inert and non-absorbable.

explanation: Silk is a braided protein suture.
It reacts markedly and is in fact very slowly absorbable despite its classification.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Silk is the exception among 'non-absorbables'.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about tensile strength is correct?

options.text: A wound reaches full strength by 3 weeks
options.why: At 3 weeks it has only ~20% of final strength.

options.text: A wound never regains full original strength
options.why: Correct.

options.text: Scar is stronger than intact skin
options.why: Scar is weaker than intact tissue.
Remodelling continues about a year.

options.text: Collagen I is laid down before collagen III
options.why: Collagen III precedes collagen I.

explanation: Remodelling raises strength over about a year.
But the wound never regains its full original tensile strength.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Repaired tissue is permanently weaker.

mcqs.stem: Which is NOT a recognised risk factor for pressure sores?

options.why: A key risk factor.
A recognised risk factor.
Correct — denervation (loss of sensation), not good innervation, is the risk.
A recognised risk factor.
A recognised risk factor.

explanation: Risk factors include immobility, poor nutrition, anaemia, denervation and soiling.
Intact sensation is protective, so 'good innervation' is not a risk factor.
keyFacts: Denervation (not good innervation) predisposes to pressure sores.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Loss of protective sensation drives pressure injury.

mcqs.stem: Alginate dressings are:

options.text: Derived from seaweed and gel with exudate
options.why: Correct.
That describes some occlusive films, not alginates.
That describes osmotic agents like honey.
That is VAC.
Not the defining property of alginates.

explanation: Alginates come from seaweed.
On contact with exudate they form a fibrous gel and a moist bed.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Alginates suit exudative wounds.

mcqs.stem: A wound over the shin of the tibia heals with very little contraction. The best explanation is:

options.why: Vitamin C aids, and its excess is not the issue.

options.text: Adhesion of the wound to bone
options.why: Correct — adhesion to a bony surface prevents contraction.
Immobilisation helps healing.
The shin has relatively poor supply, and vascularity would aid healing.
Not the described mechanism.

explanation: Contraction needs mobile soft tissue.
Adhesion to underlying bone (e.g. over the shin) prevents it.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Fixed wounds contract poorly.

mcqs.stem: Which open wound has the highest inherent risk of infection due to contamination and devitalised tissue?

options.why: Clean, minimal tissue destruction, lower infection risk.
Correct — irregular, devitalised, contaminated, high infection risk.
Superficial, cleaned easily.
A closed injury with intact skin.
Clean and controlled.

explanation: Lacerations are caused by blunt violence.
They are devitalised and contaminated with a high infection risk.
keyFacts: Lacerated wounds are dirty and devitalised.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Mechanism predicts contamination.

mcqs.stem: Healing by primary intention is characterised by:

options.why: That is secondary intention.

options.text: Minimal fibrosis and a fine scar
options.why: Correct.
That is secondary intention.
That is tertiary intention.
Even primary intention leaves a fine scar.

explanation: Primary intention apposes clean edges immediately.
Healing shows minimal fibrosis and a neat scar.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Apposed clean edges scar least.

mcqs.stem: Regarding nerve and tendon injury within a contaminated wound, the correct principle is:

options.why: Contaminated wounds should have repair deferred.
Correct — defer nerve/tendon repair in contamination.
They can be repaired later once clean.

options.text: Repair only the nerve, never the tendon
options.why: Both are deferred, not selectively repaired.

options.text: Close the deep fascia over them
options.why: Deep fascia is left open in contamination.

explanation: Clean incised wounds allow primary nerve/tendon repair.
In contamination, repair is deferred until the wound is clean.
keyFacts: Defer nerve/tendon repair in a dirty wound.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Timing of repair depends on contamination.

mcqs.stem: Granulation tissue is composed of:

options.why: Mature collagen predominates later, in remodelling.
Correct.
Those dominate the earlier inflammatory clot.
Epithelium migrates over the surface, separate from granulation tissue.
Debris is removed, not the tissue itself.

explanation: Endothelial buds plus fibroblasts form granulation tissue.
It later matures into fibrous tissue.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Granulation tissue is the building phase.

mcqs.stem: Which is the strongest and most inert suture, used to close a sternotomy?

options.why: Reactive and slowly absorbable.
Correct — very high tensile strength, very inert, used for sternotomy.
Braided absorbable, not for sternotomy.
Absorbable and obsolete.
Good strength but not the sternotomy choice.

explanation: Steel has very high tensile strength and is very inert.
It is used to close the sternum after cardiac surgery.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Match extreme-strength needs to steel.

mcqs.stem: A scar overlying the elbow gradually shortens and limits extension. This is best described as:

options.why: Keloid overgrows the wound but does not primarily limit joint movement by shortening.
Correct — pathological scar shortening across a joint causing deformity.
Raised within margins; does not by definition limit the joint.
That is wound breakdown.
Normal scars do not contract to limit a joint.

explanation: A scar crossing a joint can shorten pathologically.
This contracture causes deformity; correct joint positioning during healing minimises it.
keyFacts: Contracture crosses a joint and deforms it.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Position joints correctly while a scar matures.

mcqs.stem: The typical colour sequence of a resolving contusion is:

options.why: This is the reverse order.
Correct — extravasated blood breaks down.
Not the described sequence.
Not typical of a simple contusion.
A contusion changes colour as blood degrades.

explanation: Extravasated blood is bluish initially.
As haemoglobin breaks down it turns brown then green.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Bruise colour tracks blood breakdown.

mcqs.stem: Which best defines a chronic wound?

options.why: Pain does not define chronicity.

options.text: A wound failing to heal in a reasonable time (~3 months)
options.why: Correct.

options.text: A wound closed by primary intention
options.why: That is an acute clean wound.

options.text: A wound less than 2 weeks old
options.why: That is acute.
Site does not define chronicity.

explanation: Chronic wounds miss the normal healing timeline.
The usual threshold is about three months, with shared local hypoxia.
keyFacts: Chronic = fails to heal within ~3 months.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Time and arrest define chronicity.

mcqs.stem: Which is the correct pairing of wound and depth relationship?

options.why: Incised wounds are longer than deep.
Correct.
Abrasions are superficial.
A contusion is closed.
Missile wounds are deep, high-energy.

explanation: Penetrating wounds have a small opening but reach deep.
They are deeper than long — hence hidden deep injury.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Depth-to-length ratio flags hidden injury.

mcqs.stem: The main purpose of a wound dressing is to:

options.why: Dressings limit but do not guarantee sterility.

options.text: Provide the ideal environment for healing and limit bacterial overgrowth
options.why: Correct.
Dressings do not replace debridement.

options.text: Provide tensile strength to the wound
options.why: Sutures, not dressings, provide strength.
Not the primary purpose.

explanation: Dressings optimise the local environment.
They support healing and limit bacterial overgrowth.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Dressings manage the wound micro-environment.

mcqs.stem: Irradiated tissue heals poorly mainly because:

options.why: Irradiation reduces, not increases, healthy repair.
Correct.
Irradiation reduces vascularity.
The opposite occurs.
Infection is not the primary mechanism.

explanation: Radiation damages small vessels.
Endarteritis obliterans produces ischaemia that impairs contraction and granulation.
mcqs.teachingPoint: Radiation impairs healing via vessel damage.

emqs.instruction: For each description, select the single most likely wound type.

stems.stem: A clean straight wound from a knife, longer than deep, with brisk bleeding.
stems.why: Sharp-blade cuts are clean and longer than deep.

stems.stem: An irregular, devitalised, contaminated thigh wound after a road traffic accident, with skin sheared off the deep fascia.
stems.why: Blunt severe violence gives a lacerated, often degloving, wound.

stems.stem: A small deep track from a screwdriver with a tiny external opening and poor drainage.
stems.why: A pointed object gives a deeper-than-long wound with a small opening.

stems.stem: A wound where damage occurs far from the visible entry track, with cavitation.
stems.why: High-energy transfer causes cavitation and remote damage.

emqs.instruction: For each situation, select the single most appropriate suture.

stems.stem: Closure of the abdominal wall and a hernia repair needing a durable inert monofilament.
stems.why: Prolene is the inert monofilament of choice for the abdominal wall/hernia.

stems.stem: A slow-absorbing monofilament for a mass abdominal closure.
stems.why: PDS is the slowest-absorbing absorbable, ideal for slow-healing closure.

stems.stem: A braided absorbable suture for a bowel anastomosis.
stems.why: Vicryl is a braided absorbable used for GI anastomoses.

stems.stem: Closure of a sternotomy after open-heart surgery.

emqs.instruction: For each vignette, select the single most likely diagnosis.

stems.stem: A painless ulcer under the metatarsal head of a diabetic foot at a pressure point.
stems.why: Neuropathic ulcers occur at pressure points and are painless.

stems.stem: A shallow ulcer in the gaiter area with surrounding pigmentation; the commonest leg ulcer.
stems.why: Venous ulcers are commonest and sit in the gaiter area.

stems.stem: A long-standing ulcer that now has raised, everted edges and will not heal.
stems.why: Malignant (squamous) change gives heaped, everted edges.

stems.stem: A sacral ulcer in a bedridden patient with full-thickness loss short of the fascia.
stems.why: Sustained pressure over a bony prominence causes a pressure sore.

emqs.instruction: For each statement, select the single best-matching term.

stems.stem: Contains smooth-muscle actin and reduces wound size.
Immature collagen deposited first, later replaced.
stems.why: Collagen III is laid down before collagen I.

stems.stem: Covers a clean sutured wound in about 48 hours.
New capillary buds plus fibroblasts filling the wound.

summary: Wound healing runs through haemostasis/inflammation (~5 days, macrophage-led), proliferation (granulation tissue and epithelial migration) and maturation (collagen III → I over ~1 year, never regaining full strength). Wounds heal by primary, secondary or tertiary (delayed primary) intention. Healing is slowed by general factors (age, poor nutrition, vitamin C/A deficiency, diabetes, steroids) and local factors (poor vascularity, infection, tension, foreign body, irradiation); immobilisation helps. Know hypertrophic scar (within margins) versus keloid (beyond margins), and contracture across joints. Classify open wounds by mechanism, always suspecting deep injury in penetrating/missile trauma, and follow the contaminated-wound rule: no nerve/tendon repair, leave deep fascia and skin open. The commonest chronic leg ulcer is venous; grade pressure sores by depth; prefer monofilament (Prolene) for the abdominal wall and match dressings to exudate and infection.
